title: Artists are quitting Instagram and Facebook over fears AI will steal their work | CNN Business
text:
Source: CNN

Matty Burnham, a watercolor artist in the United Kingdom, said he discovered a Pinterest account impersonating his illustration in 2024. The account created AI versions of his watercolors and listed them on fake profiles via Shopify, Facebook and Instagram, he told CNN.

Although Burnham tracked the Pinterest account to HoChi Min City, Vietnam, he does not know who was behind it.

It’s part of a wave of AI-generated artwork that’s taking business away from the creators themselves, and is especially prevalent on Meta-owned Instagram and Facebook. CNN spoke with over a dozen artists on how they are navigating the current AI landscape.

AI-generated art profiles “monetize Facebook,” Burnham said. “They have hundreds of thousands of followers who believe these fake profiles are genuine artists anddirect users to various websites with shops and ads.”

The problem has pushed some independent artists to pull back from Instagram, Facebook and other Meta platforms, especially with the tech giant’s proposed updates to its terms of service. Some have considered leaving Meta-owned social media platforms entirely, pausing posting or turning to other online creator communities such as Patreon or Substack.

Tim O’Brien, board member at the Society of Illustrators, said he believes artists deserve meaningful consent, fair compensation and accessible ways to challenge unauthorized exploitations of their work.

“For many artists, this is not merely a legal dispute. It is a question of livelihood, creative ownership, consent and basic fairness,” O’Brien said.

Meta’s updated terms would still allow automated software to scrape external websites and extract large amounts of data without permission from business account owners. This includes personal portfolios, online stores, and links to Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads business accounts.

The terms were originally supposed to go into effect October 30, then got pushed back to November 20. The companyannouncedon November 5 that the updates were delayed indefinitely.

“We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect,” a Meta spokesperson said in a statement to CNN.

Still, even with the latest delay, the proposed updates have already caused anotherwaveof artists to leave Meta.

Samantha Waldron, co-owner of Dutcher Photography in Madison, Wisconsin, told CNN that she deletedall business and personal Facebook pages earlier this month and has since transitioned her Instagram business accounts to personal accounts, deleted a vast majority of posts, and removed all external website links from Meta account bios.

“It was the last straw that was a long time coming. I’m frankly relieved not to have to worry about keeping up on social media moving forward,” said Waldron.

Under the updated terms, independent artists’ images, style, and property could be scraped without their knowledge to train generative AI models, creators told CNN. Those AI models could then replicate or replace human-made art — and potentially impact artists’ businesses on those sites.

Megan Wimberley, founder of Cowgirl Artists of America in Tulsa, Oklahoma, is in the process of deleting all of her Meta accounts. She told CNN that she considers these new terms a major breach of trust. Wimberley believes everyone – not just artists – should be concerned about posting their personal images, video and audiodue topotential AI scraping.

“I actually view Meta as a company trying to lead the way in AI and that their social media platforms are no longer really about social media but more about free licensing to train their AI,” said Wimberley. “If you’re a mother and you’re posting your children, you’re potentially licensing Meta to use your children to train their AI.”

Some even chose to“go dark”on Meta platforms from October 30 through November 6 when the updated Meta terms were initially planned to kick in, refraining from posting or sharing content in protest of the updated terms. Wimberley said she started the“Meta blackout”campaign on October 22, and it took off from there.

Nicole McKay, artists relations director at The Guild of Artists and Artisans, told CNN in a statement that many artists in the United States have begun removing their accounts from Meta platforms in response to the upcoming policy change with AI model training. Many artists have posted “goodbye” messages on Instagram and Facebook, citing Meta’s politics.

“For artists who rely on these platforms to showcase and sell their work, connect with customers, and build their businesses, leaving Meta presents a difficult choice between protecting their work and maintaining their livelihoods,” McKay said.

AI-generated artwork has serious repercussions on the creator economy, artists told CNN. Online imitators are forcing artists to change their strategy on how they reach an audience.

Andrew Scott, a contemporary artist in Rochester, New York, said he directly messaged an AI art impersonator in September about copying his work.

He said the person admitted to using Scott’s original work as a starting point to build her own AI-generated art videos. The person behind theimpersonating profilethen shared AI clips on Instagram, giving the impression she created the actual art. Scott noted one of her posts with AI artworkreceived 50 million views.

Scott said he explained to the impersonator how the AI versions could potentially hurt his business. She has since unfollowed him on social media but continues to create the AI-prompted knockoffs, he said.

Nancy Chen, a ceramic artist in Canada, posts videos on social media that show how she makes sale pieces. But she understands those clips could also be vulnerable to AI model training. Chen says she’s been wary lately of posting polished images of her work on Meta platforms but hasn’t decided to leave yet.

“It makes me wonder how independent artists can present their work to the world when their transparency can be weaponized,” Chen told CNN. “AI can outpace any individual artist, so I definitely feel some pressure to compete in price, even though I feel my labor is already underpriced.”

One of the main concerns for creators is the scale and speed that AI can push content, especially compared to human-made work that can be time-consuming. That concern is compounded by questions of how generative AI is trained on artwork, usually without artists’ say, and how copyright law applies to AI.

Isaiah Steinfeld, an American Institute of Graphic Arts Board Member who builds with AI, said that protecting artists and embracing the technology don’t have to be opposing views. He noted that artists can still register work for copyright, pursue infringement claims and get unauthorized copies taken down.

For instance, Meta said creators can report instances of AI impersonators and submit takedown requests via its Intellectual Property Reporting Center.

“So, provenance has to cut both ways: protect creators from having their work appropriated and protect people using new (AI) tools from having their actual contributions erased,” Steinfeld said.

Google released an online tool,SynthID Detector, this month to the public. The free site allows anyone to upload a file to check if that image, video or audio file was made by AI from Google and partners such as OpenAI, Nvidia and Kakao.

In a press release, Google said the platform has watermarked over 180 million images and video and regularly sees over a million verification requests each day.

But this is only the beginning, and independent artists agree these changes do not go far enough. Many still grapple with whether to share content on social platforms at all, but in their line of work, it’s about brand awareness.

“Personally, I don’t trust that there will be enough done to protect artists,” Burnham said. “The UK government seems more concerned about not limiting profitable start-up tech companies than protecting artists. My hope is that the public continues to reject gen-AI in this current model.”

When CNN reached out for comment, a spokesperson for the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said: “The government has engaged extensively with creatives, industry bodies and AI firms and we are taking time to ensure we find the right approach to this issue.”

“We have been clear that we will not proceed with any course of action which does not work for our creative industries and our AI sector,” they added.
